summary:
Consensual same-sex conduct between men is lawful. The High Court struck down the colonial-era "carnal knowledge" offence, Penal Code Section 164(a) and (c), on 11 June 2019 in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General, and the Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 29 November 2021, writing that such laws "incentivise law enforcement agents to become key-hole peepers and intruders into the private space of citizens." The repealed paragraphs were formally struck from the statute book in March 2026 by the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026.

Section 167, which criminalises sexual conduct between women, was not removed by that litigation and has not been repealed by the legislature. In the Universal Periodic Review of May 2023 (43rd session), Botswana declined Canada's recommendation to repeal Section 167.

Enforcement against gay men was historically rare. The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report found that police "did not target same-sex activity" and recorded no reported violence based on sexual orientation or gender identity that year, while documenting societal discrimination against LGBT people. Former President Festus Mogae told the BBC that he had instructed police not to arrest or harass gay people during his ten years in office, while declining to change a law he said would cost him an election.

Official rhetoric has also included open hostility. In February 2011 the Deputy Speaker of the National Assembly said he would have those who practise homosexuality killed if he had the power. President Ian Khama deported the American anti-gay pastor Steven Anderson in September 2016, stating "we don't want hate speech in this country." In November 2018 President Mokgweetsi Masisi said people in same-sex relationships "have been violated and have also suffered in silence for fear of being discriminated" and deserved protection. LEGABIBO and activists called the government's decision to appeal the 2019 decriminalisation ruling an "affirmation of persistent homophobia and transphobia."

Legal gender recognition has been won case by case rather than granted by statute. In September 2017 the High Court held that the Registrar of National Registration's refusal to change a transgender man's gender marker violated his constitutional rights to dignity, privacy, freedom of expression, equal protection, freedom from discrimination and freedom from inhumane and degrading treatment, and ordered the state to amend his documents from female to male. In December 2017, after a four-year legal battle, the trans woman and activist Tshepo Ricki Kgositau obtained a female identity card, the first such order in the country; she dedicated the victory to "every single trans diverse person in Botswana." No administrative process exists: in the May 2023 Universal Periodic Review Botswana declined Canada's recommendation to introduce one, the outcome document recording that a clear administrative process was yet to be introduced.

A constitutional argument against discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is available. In June 2019 the High Court ruled that "sex" in Section 3 of the Constitution must be "generously and purposively interpreted" to include sexual orientation; legal commentator Carmel Rickard assessed that this gives LGBT Batswana a stronger constitutionally based argument against discrimination.

A draft constitutional amendment circulated in 2024 would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities. In June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct. Civic groups criticise the wider review process. The fate of the draft is not resolved in the sources reviewed.

Community infrastructure exists and is legally protected. A 2016 Court of Appeal order requiring the state to register LEGABIBO established freedom of association, expression and assembly for the organisation; LEGABIBO now runs advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health and HIV work, and publishes Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources.

Implementation of the判 judgments has been contested. In May 2024 the Southern Africa Litigation Centre assessed that although the 2016, 2017 and 2021 precedent wins are on the books, implementation "has not been satisfactory so far."

Public attitudes are divided but shifting. Afrobarometer recorded the share of respondents welcoming or not being bothered by a homosexual neighbour rising from 43% in 2016 to 50% in 2021.
tangentialFactors:
The decriminalisation litigation and the gender-recognition rulings form part of a wider set of constitutional precedents in Botswana, alongside the 2016 Court of Appeal order on LEGABIBO's registration, which the Southern Africa Litigation Centre treats as a single body of wins whose implementation is assessed jointly across Botswana and a neighbouring jurisdiction.

Botswana's trajectory differs from that of the neighbouring jurisdiction covered in the same litigation, where the equivalent precedent has faced a more contested political response; the Southern Africa Litigation Centre's 2024 assessment treats implementation failure as a shared regional problem rather than a Botswana-only one.

The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report, the source for the finding that police did not target same-sex activity that year, is a broad country report whose wider assessment covers violence against women, prison conditions and discrimination against the San; its LGBT section is the part with direct bearing on trans and LGBT visitors.

Draft constitutional reform in 2024 proceeded through a process that civic organisations publicly criticised, so an intersex-specific protection clause advancing does not by itself indicate a settled expansion of non-discrimination coverage.
localsOnly:
Section 167 remains on the statute book and continues to expose women who have sex with women to criminal liability; the legislature has not acted on the 2023 Universal Periodic Review recommendation to repeal it.

Residents seeking legal gender recognition must litigate individually. There is no registrar-level or administrative route, and each case produces a court order bound to its own facts rather than a general entitlement.

LEGABIBO operates as locally rooted infrastructure: it ran a World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong, and maintains Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources for residents, alongside its advocacy and sexual-health and HIV programmes. Its registration was compelled by the 2016 Court of Appeal order on freedom of association, expression and assembly.

Public tolerance among residents has risen but remains below a majority in the survey evidence: 43% in 2016 to 50% in 2021 welcomed or were not bothered by a homosexual neighbour.

Residents have also been the audience for political statements of both kinds. The Deputy Speaker's February 2011 threat to have homosexuals killed, President Khama's 2016 deportation of Steven Anderson, President Masisi's November 2018 acknowledgement of violations suffered by people in same-sex relationships, and former President Mogae's account of instructing police not to arrest or harass gay people are all statements made to a domestic audience.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory documents the repeal of Penal Code Section 164(a) and (c) through a judgment, appeal and a March 2026 statute-book rectification order, but the primary text of the Rectification of the Laws (Penal Code) Order, 2026 was not reviewed here; the claim rests on a secondary encyclopedic source and should be checked against the Government Gazette.

Whether the 2026 rectification order touched Section 167, or any other Penal Code provision relevant to trans visitors, is not resolved in the sources reviewed.

No sourced material in the inventory addresses how prisoners are housed by gender identity, access to hormone therapy or trans-related healthcare in state facilities, airport or border screening that could reveal a trans status, or rules on entry and visa issuance in relation to a mismatch between passport and presented gender.

The status of the 2024 draft constitutional amendment, including whether the intersex and disability discrimination provisions were adopted, is unresolved in the sources reviewed.

No data was available on the use of Section 167 in prosecutions, on outcomes for trans complainants in assault or police-engagement cases, or on whether the 2017 gender-recognition orders have been applied to any further applicant.
